items.body:
Bassbin auteur Martyn’s knack for album craft is clear on his refined yet expansive 5th solo LP, landing 8 years since ‘Voids’ with eight diverse cuts that ideally portray his strength in jazz-rooted diversity, developing binds with a range of distinctive instrumentalists and voices: Duval Timothy, Lucinda Chua, Musa Okwonga among them.

It's an unexpected one - but give it a minute. While the late-album collaboration with tenor sax don Cisneros sounds like a weighty modern jazz flex that could have been snatched from any number of Dusty Groove-cosigned reissues, and the moonlit 'Remnants', featuring Chua on cello and Timothy on piano, sounds as if it's been purpose built for an A24 soundtrack, Martyn's personality shines through when the various threads are knotted together. The D.C.-based Dutchman has admired jazz from a distance for decades and seems to understand its impact on his craft; just check 'Hypnotoxic Laser', a slow, jungle-inspired roller that harks back to the best early Photek gear, or the album's impressive lead single 'Heavy Sound', that imagines what Martyn's taut post-dubstep might sound like if it was played by a jazz quartet. 

His one-on-one collaboration with Timothy, 'No One Plays The Game', is a good opportunity to hear those unmistakably airy harmonies juxtaposed with very different sonics and 'Phantom Jazz' is an impressive diversion too, an update of Skalpel's dimly lit formula with drums from Mischa Porte.

Abstract dub dream-weavers SKRS INTL. & WZRDRY remerge at the behest of Bristol’s Accidental Meetings for a super lush dose of wormholing ambient dance pressure tipped FFO Rezzett, Peak Oil/False Aralia, Second Woman.

‘Orbit Flares’ combines the two Canadian units for the first time in over a decade, naturally reprising an empathic level of vibes in a half hour of music that betrays illusive tekkerz developed over the interim. Any semblance of sharp edges are smudged to a brilliantly psychedelic, polychromatic lustre and laced with disciplined, yet properly wayward rhythms that tumble, buckle and vaporise in fractious delirium. Each new SKRS drop is welcome around ours but, jeez, they really push into their most impressive work here, possibly thanks to wzrdryAV’s synaesthetic suss.

Front to back it feel likes they catch minds/bodies in the split second before going under anaesthesia, and extrude us into pitch-bent helical vortices of plonging dub chords and gooey bass, finding bold new realms of computerised dub suss. Handrails are slippery as fuck, ground melts beneath feet, leaving bodies gyring in space between the weightless dub techno inflections of ‘1.1’, into air-stepping chicanery on ‘1.2’, or glitching like a hair-kissing Vladislav Delay on ‘1.3’. The smeared chords and scudding subs of ‘2.1’ call to mind Second Woman emulating the illusive dub-soul of False Aralia drops, and ‘2.3’ feels like distant rig heard on a Nitrous-induced permo. 

Sheer class for harder to please future dub freaks.

Xiu Xiu reprise their Lynch reverence with a suitably bleak, beguiling take on the ‘Eraserhead’ score, nearly a decade after their ‘Twin Peaks’ homage became a surprise hit. The inimitable ‘70s flick’s industrial imagery and concrète score, arranged by Lynch with Alan Splet, prompts Jamie Stewart and co. to some truly discomfiting yet enigmatic work that arguably lives up to the legendary director’s vision.

"In 2016, with the blessing of David Lynch and Angelo Badalamenti, Xiu Xiu released and toured the surprisingly successful album and concert, Plays the Music of Twin Peaks. Out of respect and deference to the beloved series, the band decided to put the concert to rest in 2018. 

After the recent and untimely passing of David Lynch, Xiu Xiu began to receive several high-profile requests to revive their interpretation of this iconic music. However, in wanting to always try to follow, honor, and continue to be inspired by the incredibly high bar of artistic challenge set by Lynch, Xiu Xiu is instead going deeper. 

The album itself is a masterpiece in sound collage and experimentation, with tracks like “Tetra” and “Sleep Synth” shifting from minimal auditory sensations to a clobbering, grotesque cacophony. The album’s closing track, “In Heaven,” is a beautiful rendition of Peter Ivers’ original composition, with Stewart’s delicate and soft vocals showcasing the elegance and wonder found in Lynch’s directorial debut, Eraserhead. 

Eraserhead’s original sound design and score by Alan Splet and Lynch guide Xiu Xiu’s expanded interpretation, reflecting their influence as fans and musicians. The original film gives birth to Xiu Xiu’s visual lens, through which audiences are baffled and pummeled by the band’s imaginary unused auxiliary footage. 

Is it a short-term art installation, an exploded tribute to a cinematic triumph, an epitaph to an idol via an entirely new work? Yes. Is it intense, odd, curious, and shrouded in the gloomiest of nights? Of course. 

After all, it is Eraserhead."

"Edgar debuts on Dark Entries with Pavor, an 11 track LP of sleazy disco, warped synthpop, and gothic cumbia. Veteran musician Luis Gutierrez has spent the past two decades touring in bands, running Lalalandia Studio, and building his practice in Oakland and Guadalajara. But now, for his first solo outing, he has become Edgar, a pop star who knows no limits! “Edgar feels mightier than anyone but is always reduced to his vices” says Gutierrez, and Pavor delivers vices in spades.

From the opening salvos of “Otra Agua,” it’s clear we’re in for a wild ride: seasick synths slide along slamming disco beats, menacingly chanted vocals sit amid a flurry of careening horror movie samples. The mischief does not abate as we’re guided through a demented funhouse of genre detournements. Edgar puts his indelible fingerprints over every inch of this vinyl, from uptempo numbers like the spooky chip-tune frenzy of “Nunca Mas” to the twisted cumbia of “Panteon.” We’re even treated to a fairly faithful (and majestic) Spanish-language cover of Amanda Lear’s “Follow Me,” here titled “Sigueme.” EBM, space disco, and horror movie soundtracks all find their way into the mix on Pavor, but the diverse palette comes together perfectly, like a Yello album for the 21st century.

On Pavor, Edgar brings us a healthy dose of pure excess, reminding us that dread can be a hell of a lot of fun. "

Arvo Pärt has become something of a yardstick by which contemporary sacred music has been measured, and 'Alina' is arguably his most loved and imitated piece of work. 

Für Alina was first performed in Tallinn in 1976, and has become one of Pärt’s most-loved and widely appreciated works - regarded by many as an early, defining example of his signature tintinnabuli style. In the years since its release, Pärt has become the most performed living composer in the world, his approach to religious music seeping deep into our cultural landscape, from the avant garde to the mainstream.

Rendered with nothing more than piano and violin, this definitive ECM version from 1999 features Vladimir Spivakov, Sergej Bezrodny, Dietmar Schwalke and Alexander Malter providing alternate versions, handpicked by Pärt himself from recordings that were originally several hours long. It’s a masterclass in simplicity; an almost painfully beautiful rendering of emotional landscapes that, in the wrong hands, could have (and has, on many occasions, by so many) turned to schmaltz.

Following last year’s acclaimed ‘The Wringing Cloth’, New England-based Henry Birdsey dusts off his debut album as Old Saw for a much needed reissue, offering a stunning dose of Takoma-rooted Stars Of The Lid x Lanois-coded American Primitive, primed for high summer.

With the Old Saw project put to bed after five years and four albums, Tongue Depressor's Henry Birdsey reinvigorates his 2021 debut with a much needed new pressing, offering many a first glimpse at his earliest endeavours in the realms of windswept blues x meditative ragas. A dust-caked mass of pedal and lap steel twangs, fluttering banjo, rasping fiddle and organ hums, his influences might be familiar, but are here deployed in a mode that’s more intentional, slower, intended for deep listening. We might be able to see it through a broadly "ambient" (small a) lens in 2026, decades after Brian Eno's Americana-tinged Lanois collaborations and Laraaji releases, but we get the feeling that Birdsey's in an altogether more devotional headspace. 

As well as the obvious reference points - Fahey, Bruce Langhorne, Ry Cooder - there's also an air of CC Hennix and Catherine Lamb's hallowed minimalism wafting thru the 13-minute opener 'The Mechanical Bull at Our Lady of the Valley’. And although its music that's rooted in Americana, specifically a nostalgic vision of a past that's becoming harder and harder to reconcile with the present, Birdsey does enough to approach it through a critical lens, searching for harmonies pulled from more far-flung folk and sacred forms. On 'Chewing the Bridle’, it's hard not to hear the undercurrent of Hindustani music in the low, undulating drone notes, and 'Dirtbikes of Heaven, Grains of the Field' is a kind of contemporary praise music, lifted from the barns and mountain shacks into the clouds by Renaissance-style compositional touches. 

Gorgeous.

items.body:
Numero unearths another lost emo gem here, scraping together short-lived Delaware band Eldritch Anisette's complete recordings: a single 7" and a few additional DAT recordings that have never before seen the light of day.

Saddled with a mouthful of a name that spliced H.P. Lovecraft with French Sambuca for some reason, Eldritch Anisette only lasted a year but they did something a little different. The band sprung up from Delaware's tiny punk scene, that was gathered around Railhed drummer Nick Rotundo's Clay Creek Recording Studio. Calling themselves The Enoch Collective, the group of teens and twentysomethings shares tunes and organized cheap shows, eventually forming a sequence of different outfits. Eldritch Anisette was fronted by Clevinger's Courtney Miller and rounded out by local screamo outfit Network 34's Marc Krupanski and Tim Nichols and guitarist Allen Hitchens. And it's their fusion of influences that set them apart; Miller was driven by her interest in The Sundays and Tori Amos, while the rest of the band were circling the local punk fringe.

They played around a dozen shows, spending $100 on a session at Clay Creek and recording six tracks, three of which made it to their only release. And although the band splintered in 1997 just after the 7" appeared, their tracks are oddly resonant - edgier and weirder than most of the emo we've heard from that same period. Miller is clearly the secret weapon and it's her voice - and her charisma - that gives these songs, even the long-buried additional sessions, their bite.

‘The Dance Flo-Funk EP’ was originally cooked up by Hoermann as the 4th in a handful of 12”s on his Odic Force label, which ran between 1998-2002. It’s straight-up Detroit dancefloor sex that has led to its cult status by collectors and DJs seeking the special spice for durational sessions, hitting where it matters between the brittle, ascetic budge of ‘Dff’, the unadulterated raw baseline sleaze of ‘Woodblockpop’, a squirming tracky jack tool ‘Df’, and the tendon-tuning fidget of ‘Corecharge’.

Damn effective, damn obscure, tackle from tha D!

items.body:
Michael J. Blood executes a stunning volte-face from rugged house and soul to more intuitive, introspective, world-building ambient jazz and electroacoustic dub realms under a new moniker SEES, signifying a newfound psychoactive frisson to his work that lands him somewhere in the spiritual vicinity of Vangelis, Moodymann, Ron Trent, Pendant, Terre Thaemlitz.

‘Ampersand Curve’ initiates a brilliant new phase of work by North Manchester’s most elusive artist, best known as Michael J. Blood. His string of ruffkut club bangers as well as jams with Rat Heart & Samizdat over the past seven years, have made his records a true cult property, and now find him signed to one of the UK’s most foundational techno imprints - more of which later this year.

But under the SEES aegis, he swims in very different waters, following his instincts to use the studio-as-instrument to produce his most impressive, deep-minded work, made from - and for - the heart. Where MJB was all about off-the-cuff club jams cooked for immediacy, his new stylistic switch reveals myriad worlds of influence swirling under the hood, where interrelated spheres of spiritual jazz, dub, ambient and concrète more clearly light up his rich inner world.

As the story goes, MJB was burgled a few years back, and lost most of his studio just as the project was hitting its stride. It prompted a personal review of his practice, re-learning new kit, allowing him to bend the rules. Adopting a sort of first thought, best thought approach to composition, the new methodology fuelled a renewed imagination in flux, or what he identifies as SEES: a personalised way of conveying complex emotions.

That un-doing of musical and mental conditioning opens the walls of his music to vast new horizons. Opener ‘Ithaca’ fathoms sonorous midnight jazz with 10 mins of a plangent, searching sax solo in HD widescreen, like some alternate version to the Blade Runner Love Theme, while a resonant vocoder soliloquy ‘Unseem’ reaches into space harmonised between Alvin Lucier and Ron Trent, and ‘Sheer’ chases the devil out of labyrinthine dub dimensions. The floating dream architecture of ‘Caprices’ caps the LP’s underlying narrative and painterly qualities with a romantic conclusion of blushing pads and shivered, metallic echoes of the subtropical that suggest a coming-to-terms with worries, refreshed and good to go again.

A huge, heartfelt tip for a 2026 stunner.

items.body:
KILLER second LP from Lucid Dreams paying dues to Bristol’s rich trip hop history, landing at the intersection of theeee moodiest OG 90’s blueprints x fwd club pressure, slowed to cinematic, doom-jazzy vapours - huge tip FFO Raime, Massive Attack, Photek, Jabu, Palmskin Productions...

The Lucid Dreams handle finds Jason Luxton aka Overlook switch from inch-tight contemporary D&B into roughly-related downbeat interzones surely evoking a nocturnal Bristol for anyone raised on Tricky, Portishead or Massive Attack classics. Seemingly crafted by candlelight and bathed in opiated atmosphere, the album unfurls a midnight soundscape in considerable depth across 15 parts in 64 minutes - plenty time to roll one (or two) and luxuriate in the LP’s carefully plotted course of dub-swept, smudged bass ’n drums and smoky pall.

Like Raime before him, Lucid Dreams ideally inhabits a certain dark slipstream of intrigue that riddles post-punk thru to trip hop and its downbeat descendents, but also factored with a feel for D&B’s psychoacoustic spatial engineering that is key to his music’s appeal. Exquisite attention is paid to the dusty jazz drums and low register spectres shapeshifting its cloistered structures from the Bohren-pced doom shuffle of ‘Smoke & Mirrors’ up to what feels like dark echoes of proto-Goa or sci-fi scores in ‘Reincarnation’.

His noirish ‘Reverie’ plays out like a Tricky witching hour special, and ‘Clairvoyance’ feels like Photek or SD on 33-not-45, next to dankest Wild Bunch/early Massive Attack nod ‘Slow-Wave’, and ‘Sleepwalking’ balances Flying Saucer Attack and ‘Mezzanine’ vibes, whilst ‘Transcendence’ holds a fine line of weightless ‘90s noir tension into the high plains drift of a ‘Realisation’ recalling aspects of Memotone’s ‘Warm Shadows’.

A real sleeper gem.

items.body:
20th Anniversary edition of Cat Power’s "The Greatest".

"For "The Greatest", Chan Marshall returned to Memphis, pursuing the slinky Hi Records sound of the 70s, famed for its sensuous feel and beguiling rhythms. She got Al Green’s guitarist and songwriting partner Mabon “Teenie” Hodges to play guitar on the whole album (Teenie co-wrote “Love and Happiness” and “Take Me to the River,” among other soul classics). With Teenie came his Hi Rhythm bandmate (and brother) Leroy “Flick”Hodges, who plays on half of the album (Memphis A-team bassist Dave Smith supplements). Anchoring the band is Steve Potts, whose reputation on drums was solidified when the surviving members of Booker T. and the MG’s asked him to replace their late drummer, Al Jackson. Other top Memphis musicians guest on key-boards, horns and strings. Cat Power went right to the sources, and created her own paean to the songs and styles she grew up on.

The Greatest adds to Cat Power’s singular sound all the elements that make an Al Green record great: Memphis horns, funky string arrangements, smooth background vocals. “Lived in Bars” is a hypnotic song that seems to start in the middle of the night and flow backward like water upstream to the source of a good time. Many songs hearken back to earlier in Cat Power’s career, like the surface simplicity of “Willie”—much more complicated upon deeper listen—and like “Where Is My Love,”which sounds like it could be the first song she ever wrote, and also the one to which she has always aspired. “Living Proof,” on the other hand, has an almost gospel-like swing that stands in contrast to the quieter songs. The ethereal title track is the missing link between Big Star3rd and the 21st century."

Brooklyn's Frances Chang foreshadows her third album with an EP of brittle and baroque bedroom pop. RIYL Wendy Eisenberg, Julia Holter or Cate Le Bon.

With 'been thinking bout confession' on the horizon, Chang teases a few of the key tracks, including the charming piano led 'I can feel the waves', that's maybe the most obvious line in to the whole record. Chang wrote the album on an old baby grand in her Sunset Park apartment, and that's the first sound we hear, before it's broken up by clattering drum machine samples, oddball strings and Chang's soft, effective vocals. Her songs are deceptively simple, sounding like insider's outsider music - packed out with earworms but disrupted by unusual production choices and intricate orchestrations.

items.body:
A note from Oliver and James

"Shaking off the uneasy depths of Lapsed Gasps took a minute (those mix sessions were intense!). Oliver and I knew we’d like the record that followed to let in some light. Not much light, but enough to differently illuminate the darkened corners Push For Night prefers to inhabit. So we shifted the stone slab covering the conceptual entrance to the sarcophagal room that contains the idea of PFN, just a little, and the crepuscular light inside the room changed. The shadows behaved differently, sounded differently. The textures, sizes, shapes, and acoustics of our weird space altered. How can we interpret the shadows’ song and dance differently this time? In these subtle changes in perception there lies a wealth of things to investigate, to peer into, to be afraid of, to be excited by… That said, our writing process doesn’t involve too much premeditated verbal back and forth. We tend to start lobbing sessions at each other and a path inevitably clears.

In this case, and in no small part, the clearing of the path of That Porous Line begins with the contributions of my longtime sonic comrade David Daniell. The two pieces Oliver and I made with David are the earliest in the sessions that would become this record. He brought, for lack of a better word, a beauty - a gentle, organic beauty - that ultimately reoriented PFN toward a sense of the melodic and of spontaneity. We moved away from programming sequences, generative patches, and atomizing every sound source via heavy processing. We lightened the gloom a bit. It might sound naive, but we touched instruments again; we played guitars and basses and keyboards and percussion, fingers on metal wire and wood. We reveled in less-than-perfect real time performance, and documented it as such. There is a certain lightness to that.

Don’t get me wrong, That Porous Line is absolutely a collaged, flickering, chaotic, electro-acoustic record. The project is the project after all. Although our tomb-room isn’t fully hermetic (what is?), I think it is a place PFN will always reside. A total escape outside into harshly lit reality without mystery is fairly unappealing, for us anyway. Inside is personal, guarded from too much light; a dark terrarium of weird ghosts and peculiar shadows ripe for conjuring and harnessing in order to make them kick and howl in a way pleasing to us. Or at least be near enough to them to try and hear what they sing. That’s the motive. We decorate the cave, invite the specters to reveal a message, and try to capture something. Inside, cocooned in the semi-dark of our uncommon space, we bang our heads against the act of interpreting these shifty, chimeric, hidden sonic shadows. How big is it in here? How much further down can we go? Did something move in that corner over there? Can it touch us? Can we catch it? That’s where the fear is. That’s where the fun happens. That’s why we listen. That’s why we play."

items.body:
Gilberto Gil’s debut album Louvação originally released in 1967 on Philips Records.

"Arriving on the eve of Tropicalismo, the record places Gil’s guitar at the center of rich arrangements by Carlos Monteiro de Souza, Dori Caymmi, and Leonardo Bruno. Blending samba, bossa nova, carnival traditions, and Northeastern Brazilian rhythms, the album explores social, political, and religious themes. The title track “Louvação,” co-written with Torquato Neto, calls for collective awareness, while “A Rua” carries a bittersweet nostalgic tone. Gil’s deep connection to Bahia flows through “Beira-Mar” (with Caetano Veloso), and his poetic imagination shines in “Lunik 9,” reflecting on the space race. “Ensaio Geral” captures the political energy of carnival, while “Rancho da Rosa Encarnada” (with Torquato Neto and Geraldo Vandré) evokes traditional festivities. Highlights include the rhythmically inventive “Roda,” the celebratory “Viramundo” (with Capinan), and the nostalgic “Água de Meninos.” The romantic “Maria (Me Perdoe, Maria)” offers a moment of intimacy, while “Procissão” closes the album with a powerful reflection on faith and society."

items.body:
Aftershock: The Seismic Impact of Dubstep, by seasoned music writer Lauren Martin.

"At the cusp of a new millennium, British electronic music was rapidly changing. Jungle and garage had broken into the mainstream, but were running out of creative gas – what fresh movement would next captivate the underground? On the outer edges of London, a small group of bass lovers had the answer. Through a new strain of subloaded beats that stripped jungle, rave, techno and garage for parts, this scene returned to the dub roots, prizing the fundamentals of soundsystem culture: bass, space and togetherness. They called it dubstep.

In Aftershock: The Seismic Impact of Dubstep, Lauren Martin charts the origins of one of the 21st century’s most innovative music genres in an oral history format. Through the testimonies of its architects and an immersive array of photography, flyers and unseen scene history, Aftershock chronicles the rise of artists like Skream, Mala, Coki, Loefah, Horsepower Productions and Rusko, as well as labels and parties such as Hyperdub, Tempa, DMZ, FWD>> and Skull Disco.

Together, this movement shook the British underground, exploded onto the internet and, within a decade, had rocked global music at unprecedented scale. Through first-hand storytelling, Aftershock is a testament to how the imagination and persistence of a few can transform culture."

items.body:
Green Gartside and co’s addictively sugary turning point album crops up for a masterclass in blue-eyed soul styles.

Upon its release in 1985, ‘Cupid & Psyche 85’ marked a radical leap for the once squat dwelling communists from new wave dreamers to chart-worthy pop pucker. Prior to this record they had markedly political and philosophical leanings set to a mix of almost folksy whims, disco and reggae lite, as found on a handful of Rough Trade releases, but with ‘Cupid & Psyche 85’ they mounted a sly assault on the charts, drawing on Green Gartside’s love of Aretha Franklin’s aching soul for a far more polished sound that would parallel the likes of Prefab Sprout’s entry to the US billboard charts.

In many ways its not hard to draw lines between Gartside and the Sprout’s Paddy McAloon; both are reclusive genius types who saw the other side of the pop machine and disliked it, and both made some of the ‘80s greatest power moves, as Scritti Politti did with the likes of ‘Absolute,’ which now uncannily reminds us of trotting around Co-Op during early lockdown (it was on their in-store radio A-list), and the natty funk of ‘Wood Beez,’ their seminal prayer for Aretha Franklin, which is coincidentally co-produced by Arif Mardin.

items.body:
Stellar new album from Dave Sumner’s Function - arguably a sequel or sibling work to Sandwell District’s seminal ‘Feed Forward’ classic - marking his first solo LP since 2013, and best in his catalogue.

Running to 17 songs and nearly 2 hours of material, ‘Existenz’ works away from puristic, kick drum-led club tools and instead limns a sort of autobiographical story of Sumner’s relationship to techno and electronic music, all framed around a Videodrome-styled (David Cronenberg also directed the album’s 1999 namesake film) kind of occult cable TV aesthetic and strong nods to his early love of ‘80s electro.

Recorded 2016-2019, ‘Existenz’ is bound to surprise anyone who thought he just made heavy club tracks, and may well highlight his role in Sandwell District’s ‘Feed Forward’ album, which is arguably the strongest comparison in terms of their shared tone of mood, diversity of texture and structure, and, ultimately, their mesmerising effect. 

In total control of his sound, Function lures us into a labyrinthine, noirish sort of electronic thriller that embarks with the nostalgic Vangelis nods of ‘Sagittarius A (Right Ascension)’ and ends up drifting away in deeply romantic technohouse style with ‘Downtown 161’. What happens in between is primed for long headphone journeys and daily commutes, as the album weaves from spellbinding electro recalling E.R.P. to lush slow house featuring Robert Owens, to proper sci-fi electronic drones, samples of The Conet Project, and even breakbeat rollers, all interwoven with his signature acid and techno ligament and shine-eyed techno spirit.

Influenced by the rhetorical style of 18th century vocal music, the inspiration for this piece came naturally to Eimear who has a background in early music and has performed alongside the organ in a variety of settings from chamber works to Bach's larger orchestral works such as St Matthew Passion. In 18th century music, the cello & organ perform a role as continuo players. Traditionally the cello and organ are both intertwined and interdependent, playing the bass line and harmonies together and providing a foundation for the rest of the ensemble while soloists come in and out.

In 'Pour Upon The Sky', Eimear and Natalia play within and without of this traditional form. Freed from the need to hold the solid ground for an ensemble, the cello and organ playfully explore the space as they pass the role of solo and continuo back and forth.

TRACK 2/SIDE B: 'The Whistling Dust' is a slow steady study of the microscopic flutters of the organs and the organ. The heart of the Telford rattles and breathes as the cello dances in and out. When Natalia & Eimear began working on these pieces in the cold January, the Telford, which seemed like it had been sitting quietly for quite some time, shook and trembled as its insides were awoken. 'The Whistling Dust' speaks to the moment when the instrument moved alive, every opened stop knob of the pipes bringing the feel of the microsounds of the machine closer and closer as the cello offers utterances of encouragement."

Mutual, leading prism-pushers Batu & Dozzy break fresh ground on duo debut ‘Exhale’, encompassing a spectra of tempos, moods & grooves in pursuit of elusive studio geists between Dozzy’s Rome facility and Batu’s peripatetic CPU.

Seeded in an ad hoc b2b DJ set at Draaimolen Festival, ’23, and cultivated over sessions at Dozzy’s hardware treasure trove in Rome, ‘Exhale’ naturally calibrates the two operators’ distinct visions on eight cuts teeming with detail and clean-hoofed for club use. Dozzy’s quarter century of obsessive, finely variegated techno tekkerz elide Batu’s signature offbeat syncopation and feel for texture within deceptively effortless designs that arguably transcend the sum of their parts. The results surely pin-point a dancefloor ideal of cyborganic sensuality and chromed out chronics that references the now, the future, while exerting mercurial sidespins on tried & tested forms.

In the artists’ own words: "It was interesting to see Omar interacting with my studio methods," explains Dozzy. "I know my machines very well. It was fun to do something out of my routine and use my machines in a different way to turn on Omar's ideas. There were a few things I was very excited to use, especially with someone who's an expert and used these instruments for a very long time," Batu reveals. "We tried lots of different tempos, different rhythmic patterns. I was excited by the direction we were taking, and getting so many ideas of where it could go."

In combination they generate a slew of rudely balanced equations, tentatively toeing glassy waters in the hyaline cavern of ‘Emergence’, locking into a swingeing Afro-acid churn on ’Spiral’, and stepping  to more angular, holographic techno on ‘Drift’, with nods to the nuance of mbalax-via-oingy boingy dubstep in ‘Off Axis’. And it only gets craftier in the 2nd half, diffusing the finest haze of cyberdub FX and palpitating subs on ‘Swarm’, training tendons to the tightest steppas techno on ‘Flicker’ and the title tune’s expansive trek, before seeing it off with a sublime update of early AI electronica in the shine-eyed swoon of ‘Bloom’.

Fêted Parisian producer GЯEG runs hard lines of bolshy UK bass and mutant Mauritian shatta with Dopeman for a standout turn on Florentino’s Club Romantico.

Symptomatic of Paris’ position as contemporary crucible of Afro-Latin club pressure, both tunes speak to the city’s interplay of classic innovations from the UK’s Caribbean diaspora with up-to-the-second accentuation of current African and South American trends. 

Lead banger ‘bby’ is a deftly hulking chunk of UK-skooled pressure, rolling out distorted, dive-bombing baseline-grime hybrid offset with kicker vocal motif and flyaway melody to supremely upfront and rugged effect. 

‘Kas Frekans’, on the other hand, trades his twyst on Mauritian shatta with the sound’s key proponent, Dopeman, at once calling to mind Coki’s mid-range dubstep snarl, moombahton’s squashed swivel and tuffest, grimiest ends of Angolan-Portuguese tarraxho.

On part 4 of 6 tapes documenting his legendary all-night set at The White Hotel, Tom Boogizm goes innnnnnn on the UKF/ballroom/Jersey club/Detroit techno axis for 90 mins of cantering, bucking, pendulous and slamming pressure.

Unleashing another sliver of his 10 hour set recorded during The White Hotel’s reopening weekend, summer ’21, this one depicts the artist also known as Rat Heart deep in his DJ flow, edging from 130BPM upwards across 90 mins of pure pressure in ceaseless swang and drive, initially simmering on a UKF tip that only gets ruggeder, screwing off into kwaito, electro-house, ballroom and Jersey club buck on the front.

Hopefully parts 5 and 6 land before TWH closes in 6 months. rip!

Back by demand - 2nd hand copies are known to trade for triple figures - Cindy’s timeless suite of sexy, hazed dream-pop is acutely tipped to anyone who holds a flame for Julee Cruise, Voice Actor, Lynch, Enya, Bianca Scout, Vince Clarke...

‘I’m Cindy’ is a chef’s kiss of effortlessly slow, seductive lo-fi songwriting that practically smushes earlobes with its heavenly marriage of Kai Hugo's faded production lustre and singer, Blue LoLãn’s range of whispered sweet nothings and harmonised coos. In the years since its original release it’s taken on a life of its own as a go-to succour for lovers of blissed-out, cinematic waft with equal measures of soft-focus, nostalgic FM synths and details that caress and crack in all the right, tender places. 

Conceptually derived from Palmbomen II’s ‘Memories of Cindy’ session of 2017, the 13 tracks find marbled whorls of sensual fascination within that LP’s fantasy reminiscence, here expanded into a spectrum of LA-via-Antwerp dream-pop like Johnny Jewel meets Alex Zhang Hungtai on the synth and sax pearl ‘Another’ or lip-smacking cruiser ‘Justin’, thru a Voice Actor-esque ‘Voice Message’ and the gossamer FM synth fronds that wrap it up on ‘Maybe Because It’s Over Now’, whilst secreting shimmers of Vince Clarke ballads in ‘2y & 6m’, and acid-laced lo-fi machine crack shades away from Maria Minerva on ’Never Let Me Go’.

No brainer!

One of those releases that makes you feel like no other music exists for a hot minute, Dean Blunt returns with a second Black Metal album for Rough Trade, delving deeper into his unfathomable yet completely approachable and direct take on visceral x melancholic folk-pop. Spoiler: It’s really fucking good.

Aided on most of the songs here by Joanne Robertson’s vocal counterpoint and Giles Kwakeulati King-Ashong’s skittering drums, these songs once again connect to AR Kane’s distinct approach to the avant grade thru imperfection. In effect, it feels like Blunt manages to squeeze all the sterile sheen out of overly tasteful music, leaving a throbbing mass of flesh, blood vessels, nerve endings - exposed and beautiful. It’s what AR Kane called ‘Kaning’ (see Dhanveer Singh Brar’s excellent 'Beefy's Tune’ book for more on this) - and effectively provides a vital riposte to a world in which so much “art" is presented and consumed as a form of numbing.

And that riposte requires no explanation - a personal narative woven with little concession to anything - there’s not even a tracklisting or credits on the physical formats, instead Blunt’s ideas are wrapped up in a succession of first grade earworms, string sections here and there, billowing subs - all melancholy, blunt smoke and bliss. 

"Flaws are discontinuities that act as tiny fissures, allowing the dim and distant, diffused gem light of pre-creation to slip thru - it is this that music existed for - a signpost, a reminder, a note.” Rudy Tambala / A.R. Kane

Black Metal 2 is as real as it gets.

items.body:
If you thought Dave Huismans’ (aka 2562, aka A Made Up Sound) recent return as ex_libris was good, his new, long-form minimalist dub special for Fergus Jones’ FELT label under the "In Transit" alias is another leap up, giving wings to nearly 40 mins of the finest shine-eyed downbeat pressure this side of NWAQ/154, Studio Pankow, Civilistjävel! or Rod Modell - proper top tier business.

In Transit sees Huismans go one step deeper down the rabbit hole he entered as ex_libris a few months ago. Like that project, it finally sees light of day after many years marinading in folders he would return to irregularly as a sort of meditative practice, dusting down loops and seeing how they connected after some dozen years hidden away in the archive.

When he finally got to unravelling them, they revealed a vibe that’s a far cry from his earliest work, and although sharing a slower, hazier aesthetic with ex_libris, he would logically push that sound deep into a sort of subconscious hypnagogia guided by sixth senses and shorn of any urgent, rhythmic impulses. The result is hugely absorbing  - deep without losing momentum, winding down different paths that feel engaging rather than forgettable.

At a rested heart rate the tracks swim on the imagination from distant, sonorous clanks and whispered chords in ‘A.33’, thru the tongue-tip thizz and searching tendrils of ‘A.2829’, to the subaquatic jazz sway of ‘A.18’, gently surfacing for air in the blissed iridescence of an ‘A.25’ shades away from NWAQ’s ‘Dead Bears’ vibes shared with the crystalline synth motifs of ‘A.19’, and vaporised to exquisite effect in ‘A.3132.’  

Special one.

items.body:
Adrian Rew's properly hypnotic cult classic 'Slot Machine Music' has finally been reissued and it sounds even more terrifying and prescient than it did back in 2013 at the height of the basement noise era. One of the best environmental recording records bar none - don't sleep.

Back in 2009, PAN released its fourth album, 'Kenrimono', a set of recordings made by Greek sound artist Ilios at Japanese pachinko halls. The sheer density of it was as shocking and as intense as anything the noise genre had to offer, packed out with whirring, crunching and chiming resonances that took you to the smokey epicenter of the Japanese gambling world. And when 'Slot Machine Music' arrived a few short years later we assumed the sound would be similar; we were wrong. Initially dropped via Rew's own Ergot Records on CDr before the great Aaron Dilloway stepped in to handle the vinyl edition on his own Hanson imprint, the album seemingly grew from the Midwestern noise petri dish - but it wasn't an exercise in aesthetic posturing, using the racket of the modern American casino to mimic the intensity of a Wolf Eyes set. Instead, Rew was drawn to the experience itself, that's been meticulously designed by malign forces to guide behavior: those trapped inside the casino's four walls are seduced into spending more, losing more and returning to do it all over again.

Rew didn't know much about the environment when he visited Cleveland's Horseshoe Casino for the first time in 2013 armed with an Olympus LS-11 recorder and a camera. And over four months, he developed a peculiar relationship with the culture, surreptitiously taping the soundscapes at various Midwestern locations - in Michigan, Indiana, Ohio and Illinois - while attempting not to lose too much cash in the process. And it's a warts-n-all set, with dialog snippets and outdoor ambiance giving us more than simply the dense mass of chimes and stings and themes that you'd hear on the casino floor itself. What Rew is able to do is create a snapshot of a time and place, capturing the sheer desolation of the casino experience and using it to drive a narrative that Robert Altman would be proud of. The first thing you notice is that each machine's sounds are in tune with the next; "game designers," explains Rew, "tune their machines to the key of C in order to optimize harmonic cohesion." So although Rew's recordings are full-bodied, they're never too chaotic or discordant. 

Indeed, if you check in for the entire record - 2013's iconic 'Slot Machine Music' and its 2014 sequel 'Slot Machine Music Vol. 2' - you'll be lulled into the same false sense of security that entrances casino regulars. It's almost like ambient music, packed out with tiny sonic details that some well-paid sound engineer-cum-neurologist worked for years to figure out. Guided meditation music? New age crypto-psychedelia? It's all here, packaged in neon-lit one-armed-bandits aimed to target the dopamine centers of aging boomers with money to burn. And the best thing about the recordings is that Rew keeps some of the chatter intact, so we can hear him tangling with casino security, or haggling with his slot machine neighbors over change. We can hear the cheers and claps as paltry sums are won while vast fortunes are lost. The best moment for us comes when Rew wanders outside Grand Victoria Casino in Elgin, Illinois at the dead of night, the crickets singing as the machines echo from behind grand double doors. A freight train rushes past and blots out any other sound, distorting the recording.

It's a good reminder that although you might be able to hide from reality inside the casino, the Midwest will inevitably confront you with its rusted truth.

items.body:
Oxfam launches label/campaign No More Radio Silence with a collaborative release featuring artists from Palestine, DRC and South Sudan.

"Artist Espoir Dekin features on our upcoming music track ‘(No More) Radio Silence’, bringing together artists connected to DRC, Palestine and Sudan, blending Afro/Arab hip-hop, industrial electronic music and spoken word into a powerful act of solidarity. Espoir uses his music to tell a story that millions of people living through conflict still face. At eight years old, he fled conflict in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), travelling through Angola, Turkey and Greece before eventually settling in the UK."

items.body:
Shakali practises signature forms of overeasy exotica on a second jag with NNF, after a gem for Good Morning Tapes, rummaging thru the ambient undergrowth between Spencer Clark fantasias, Japanese environmental and modal spiritual jazz.

"Finnish multi-instrumentalist Simo Hakalisto makes mosaic music of strings, bowls, bells, reeds, wind, water, and obscure electronics, threaded in subtle currents of color and texture. The title of his latest, Toinen Luonto (Finnish for “second nature”), alludes equally to Shakali’s earthen, tactile soundworld and Hakalisto’s deepening comfort with his craft.

The album’s eight songs feel coaxed as much as composed, a web of resonances set in motion and allowed to simmer, build, or billow. Vibrations and silences unspool and intertwine, alternately pointillist and diffuse, attuned to some hidden harmony of the spheres.

In addition to his own repertoire of rare instruments (including a 36-string kantele, built by Hakalisto’s grand-uncle), several notable collaborators contributed to Toinen Luonto: saxophonist Julian Overall; Hakalisto’s partner in the duo Lunar Horns, Timo Juntunen, playing udu and percussion; American experimentalist Roy Werner; and Belgian ambient flute samplist Les Halles."

items.body:
Potent, lysergic lounge music and psych-fonk-exotica out of Brussels, with Michael Crabbé letting everything slosh out of the lines in a real slow burn head melter, like Spencer Clark meets Giulio Erasmus and Pekka Airaksinen on some vintage Hoffmans. Another wyrd doozy from Antwerp’s reliably off-the-wall label, Souvenirs From Imaginary Cities.

“Straight from the weedy fields of swampville Bruxelles we bring you 8 ‘tranches de vie’ of deep zone-hall by weirdtronic bass veteran Michael Crabbé’s best fitting sound costume to date: the mighty Rudi J! You might know him from earlier outfits but that’s not the main issue here. Rudi J is!

When this swamp thing touches the pads, it’s off-road after three seconds, even if you’re in the middle of Europe’s capital. Mixing analog dirt and digital sound bits in a very loose and personal take on dancehall, we’re pretty far away from the dance floor but definitely swinging. It’s a trippy affair wandering around concrete flowers with a deep ambient flavor, but it’s edgy.

A hot summer fever dream following his own lusty path, full of life and wonder but with something sinister hiding around every corner. Often reaching for the stars, a deeper shade of bass keeps things nicely grounded. These sounds are built with a sound system in mind and bass culture at heart. Even if you can definitely surf on it from your couch, picking out all of its ear-pricking details, it will very much come alive on a big sound.

A layered affair with almost jazzy and orchestral elements peeping through the stereo-field, spectral and dissonant but also playful. Like early dubstep, some of these tunes can destroy a clubsound, keeping you skunking out in pedestrian mode and snorting up the atmospherics, finally forgetting about that damn phone.”
